newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK to Africa air cargo mkt competitive but quie.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK to Africa air cargo mkt competitive but quie.

text.p: Air cargo business from the UK to South Africa remains competitive amid few signs of rate changes by major carriers. It is also quieter than expected for the time of year, air cargo industry sources told Reuters.

Competition from British Airways World Cargo is still strong with one key direct carrier commenting: "BA used to be very hot on yield management but now they are just cutting rates left and right to attract business".

South Africa and Kenya are two routes where BA did not increase rates on March 17, and a company spokesman this week refuted some market suggestions that it might after all be upping its published tariffs on these routes.
Earlier on Thursday Virgin Atlantic Cargo said that it will remove with effect from April 1 its five pence a kg cargo fuel surcharge to all destinations, which took effect last November.
This was the first carrier to do so after Delta Air Lines on March 13 and the market is now awaiting a similar move by leading European airlines.

Currency factors have contributed to the quieter South African market reflecting both the weaker rand and sterling's strength, but the latter's exact impact on UK exports is still not clear, the sources said.

But despite this competition there are some signs of rates to Johannesburg firmed marginally to 1.67 stg a kg from 1.63 stg, while to Nairobi they moved to 0.95 stg a kg from 0.94. To Libreville the rate was 2.36 stg a kg against 2.35 stg previously.
A South African Airways SAA.CN cargo official said the airline is not planning any increase in ex-UK rates for the moment.
At the same time, BA's continuing discount policy was not having a major impact, as in his view, SAA:"offers a superior service where price is not the only consideration."
SAA's direct passenger and full freighter flights between North America and South Africa have also hit BA's transhipment business via London, he added.
Martinair "is seeing reasonable but not additional business and one has to be constructive on rates," said the carrier's UK cargo manager, Martin Crowe.
"We're not the cheapest nor the most expensive. Our target rate is to be in the middle of the band," he added.
"If service levels are reasonable, one will get market share ... and I'm not particularly concerned about BA," he added.

"We are not selling the same product. We provide a main dedicated freighter service, while BA is mainly bellyhold. It just not the same traffic," Crowe noted and added that sales of ex-UK palletised cargo have risen.
David Hall of ANA Aviation Services which acts as GSA for Air Gabon continued to see "very good" business on its weekly London-Gatwick to Libreville and Johannesburg Boeing 747 combi-service.
"We're carrying around 30 tonnes on each flight including five tonnes -- mainly oil industry equipment -- destined for Libreville."
ANA Aviation is also GSA for DAS Air Cargo and Hall that DAS is doing well on its outbound flights to Nairobi, Entebbe as well as Lagos: "with a lot of personal effects being carried to the latter"

Another indirect carrier to southern Africa, Air Mauritius said it is raising rates from April 1. This will see plus 45 kg moving to 1.75 stg a kg from the previous 1.65, with plus 300 kg at 1.70 stg (1.60 stg) and a tonne at 1.55 stg (1.45 stg).

The airline operates three Airbus A340 flights a week from the UK. There are Friday and Sunday flights fron Heathrow and a Monday service out of Manchester." - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+5017
